title: Cursor pagination and streaming large responses
summary: Wrap a paged API in an iterator that follows the cursor and fetches lazily; prefer cursors over offsets, which skip and repeat rows while others write. Stream big downloads to disk through a hash, with a stall watchdog instead of a total timeout.

examples.title: A paged API as an iter.Seq2 that fetches pages on demand

annotations.note: The usual page shape: the items plus an opaque cursor for the next page, absent on the last one. The client never parses the cursor; it only sends it back.
iter.Seq2 (Go 1.23) lets callers write a plain for-range over every item and never see pages. Paging and cursors stay in one function.
An error is yielded as a value, once, and then the sequence ends. That is the common convention for Seq2[T, error]: the caller decides whether to stop or log and continue.
When yield returns false the caller has left its loop (break, return, panic). The iterator must stop right there; calling yield again panics at run time.
The cursor here is just the last ID, base64-encoded so clients treat it as opaque. Real APIs often also sign or encrypt it, so they can change what's inside without breaking clients.

The IDs are Turkish licence-plate codes, and pages are ordered by ID: behind this API runs a keyset query, WHERE id > $1 ORDER BY id LIMIT 3. Ordering by name would be harder: compared byte by byte, İstanbul and İzmir sort after Konya, because İ is a two-byte character beyond ASCII. Names need a Turkish collation (golang.org/x/text/collate).
fetch is a parameter, so a fake API can stand in for the real one. In a client type it's the method that sends lesson 1's GET with a context and decodes the JSON page.
Laziness pays off: the loop stops at Bursa, the iterator returns, and the third page is never requested.

examples.title: Offset pages repeat and skip rows when the data changes; cursors don't

annotations.note: OFFSET counts positions. The returned page is a copy, as it would be after a JSON round trip; returning a subslice would let the in-place DeleteFunc below change page 1 after the fact.
A keyset cursor names the last row seen. Rows inserted before it or deleted after it can't shift the next page.

A new post at the top pushes everything down one position, so the offset client sees post 8 twice. A deleted post pulls everything up, so post 7 is never seen at all. Neither failure produces an error.

examples.title: Stream 10 MB to disk through a hash; rename only when verified

annotations.note: Write to a temp file next to the target, and rename only when the file is complete and verified. A failed download never leaves a half-written cities.csv for someone else to read.
io.Copy moves the body through one 32 KiB buffer, and MultiWriter feeds each chunk to the file and the hash, so memory stays flat whether the body is 10 MB or 10 GB. io.ReadAll would hold all of it.

Content-Digest (RFC 9530) carries a hash of the bytes as sent. A body that ends early looks like a normal end of stream to io.Copy (no Content-Length here); only the digest catches it, and the file is not renamed into place.
Each line is 30 characters but 34 bytes: İ, Ş and ı take two bytes each in UTF-8. Sizes, Content-Length and offsets are always in bytes.

examples.title: Bound stalls, not total time: a watchdog that cancels with a cause

annotations.note: A reader that wraps a reader: every chunk that arrives pushes the stall deadline back. This bounds "no progress", which is what you actually care about for a download of unknown duration.
The transfer takes 2 s, longer than the 1 s idle limit, and is never cut off: only a gap without data counts.
Clone keeps DefaultTransport's settings and adds a bound on the wait for headers. There is deliberately no Client.Timeout, which would also cut off a slow but healthy 10 GB download.
WithCancelCause (Go 1.20) lets the watchdog say why it cancelled. The Transport reports context.Cause from the body read, so the error the caller sees is errStalled, not a bare "context canceled".
The watchdog starts once the headers are in; until then the Transport's ResponseHeaderTimeout is in charge.

use_cases: Syncing every record from a SaaS API (customers, invoices, tickets) into your database
Exports and backups that are larger than the memory of the process downloading them
Infinite-scroll feeds and admin tables whose data changes while users page through it
strengths: Range-over-func iterators let a paged API look like a slice to its callers, and stop fetching when they stop reading
io.Reader composition (wrappers, MultiWriter, TeeReader) builds a streaming pipeline in a few lines, with constant memory
Keyset pagination is stable under concurrent writes and as fast on the last page as on the first
A cancel cause makes timeouts self-describing: the error says stalled, not just canceled
weaknesses: Cursors can't jump to page 37 or show a total page count; offsets can, at the cost of correctness and speed
Iterator errors need a convention (Seq2 with error), since a for-range has no error return
Streaming means the caller sees partial data before it is validated; the temp-file-and-rename discipline is on you
There's no built-in progress or stall timeout on Response.Body; you wrap the reader yourself

pitfalls.title: Reading a large body with io.ReadAll
pitfalls.detail: It holds the whole response in memory, growing the buffer by repeated reallocation along the way. Stream to the destination with io.Copy, and cap what you accept with io.LimitReader if the size is untrusted.

pitfalls.title: Writing the final file in place
pitfalls.detail: A download that fails halfway leaves a truncated file under the real name, and the next run or another process trusts it. Write to a temp file in the same directory and rename after verification, so readers see the old file or the new one, never half of one (go.files-io.writing).

pitfalls.title: Verifying a digest after transparent decompression
pitfalls.detail: If the Transport asked for gzip itself, it decompresses the body for you and deletes Content-Encoding (resp.Uncompressed is true). Your hash then covers decoded bytes, while Content-Digest covers the gzip bytes that were sent. Set Transport.DisableCompression, or request the encoding explicitly, when you verify digests.

pitfalls.title: Forgetting to stop the iterator
pitfalls.detail: An iterator that ignores yield's false return keeps fetching pages nobody reads, and calling yield after it returned false panics. Return as soon as yield says stop.

pitfalls.title: Parsing or constructing cursors on the client
pitfalls.detail: Cursors are opaque by contract; the server may change their format at any time. Store and send them back verbatim, URL-encoded.

quiz.q: A client pages through /posts?offset=N newest first. A new post is published between page 1 and page 2. What does the client see?
options: The last post of page 1 again at the top of page 2
The new post at the top of page 2
quiz.why: Everything moved down one position, so offset 3 now points at what used to be the third row. Keyset cursors don't move with positions.

quiz.q: In a for c, err := range cities(...) loop the caller hits break. What must the iterator function do?
options: Fetch the rest of the pages so the connection can be reused
Call yield once more with io.EOF
quiz.why: yield returning false means the loop is over; calling yield again panics, and the iterator should stop fetching.

quiz.q: Why is Client.Timeout a poor fit for a 5 GB download?
options: It caps the whole exchange including the body, so a slow but healthy download is cut off
quiz.why: Client.Timeout includes reading the body. A stall watchdog bounds the absence of progress instead of the total time.

quiz.q: What does io.Copy(io.MultiWriter(file, hash), resp.Body) hold in memory?
options: One buffer of a fixed size
quiz.why: Neither side implements WriterTo or ReaderFrom here, so io.Copy loops over a single 32 KiB buffer and writes each chunk to both destinations.

body:
## Concept

APIs that return collections hand them out in pages, and there are two ways to say
"the next page":

- **Offset**: `?offset=40&limit=20`, "skip 40 rows". Simple, and lets a UI jump to any
  page, but the server still reads and discards the skipped rows, and positions shift
  whenever someone inserts or deletes: rows are repeated or silently skipped.
- **Cursor (keyset)**: `?cursor=...`, where the cursor encodes the last row you saw, and
  the server continues *after* it (`WHERE id > $1 ORDER BY id LIMIT 20`). Stable under
  concurrent writes, and as fast on page 10,000 as on page 1, but only forward (and
  backward), with no "page 37".

On the client, wrap the paging in an **iterator** (`iter.Seq2[T, error]`, Go 1.23):
callers range over items, pages are fetched only as the loop asks for more, and a
`break` stops the fetching.

Large responses are **streams**. `resp.Body` is an `io.Reader`; copy it to its
destination in chunks instead of reading it into memory. Downloads get two extra
guards: write to a temp file and rename only after verifying (size, digest), and bound
*stalls* rather than total time, because a healthy 10 GB transfer may take an hour.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Python**: a generator that `yield`s items and fetches the next page inside the loop
  is exactly `iter.Seq2`; `requests.get(url, stream=True)` with `iter_content()` is the
  streaming half.
- **Java**: you would implement `Iterator<T>` or `Spliterator` (or a reactive
  `Flux`) for the pages; `InputStream.transferTo(OutputStream)` is `io.Copy`.
- **JS/TS**: an `async function*` generator consumed with `for await`, and
  `response.body` as a `ReadableStream` piped through a `TransformStream` (lesson
  ts.services.advanced). Go's version is synchronous code; the goroutine blocks, nothing
  else does.
- **C**: a `read()` loop into a fixed buffer, plus `rename(2)` for the atomic replace:
  the same design, with the error handling done by hand.

## How it works

A range-over-func loop calls the iterator once, passing `yield`; each `yield(item, nil)`
runs the loop body. A `break` in the body makes `yield` return false, and the iterator
must return then. That's how the stop propagates without channels or goroutines: the
whole thing is ordinary function calls on one stack.

In example 4, the stall watchdog is a `time.AfterFunc` that cancels the request's
context with a cause. Cancelling the context makes the Transport close the connection
and fail the pending `Read` on the body; the error the Transport reports is
`context.Cause(ctx)`, so `io.Copy` returns `errStalled` itself.

## Design notes

When you design the API (the server side), prefer cursors for anything that is written
to while being read, and make them opaque: base64 at least, signed if clients could
gain anything by forging them. Order by a unique key, or by a tuple ending in one
(`ORDER BY created_at, id` with `WHERE (created_at, id) > ($1, $2)`), or ties at page
boundaries produce the same skip-and-repeat bugs as offsets. The SQL side, including the
index that makes this fast, is in sql.indexes.stats-pagination.

On the consuming side, an iterator is the right boundary: the sync job that needs every
invoice writes `for inv, err := range client.Invoices(ctx)`, and retries (lesson 2) live
inside `fetch`. Keep the cursor of the last completed page, and a crashed sync can resume
where it stopped instead of starting over.

For downloads, decide what "done" means before starting: a byte count, a digest, or both.
Then nothing else may see the file until it is done. The same pattern (temp file, fsync
if durability matters, rename) is in go.files-io.writing.

  keyset: [10 9 8] [7 6 5]

  offset: [10 9 8] [6 5 4]
  keyset: [10 9 8] [7 6 5]
